prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Before anything could happen, flecks of real gold on her mouth, her eyes more convex than any others, the ground spoke, the barrier of lilacs spoke. What sang in the black tree was entirely gold. Her chair was empty. New absence is a great figure dark as the underskin of fruit. At the center of the earth it surrounds and amplifies the dead whose music never slows down. She came by car. I came by train. We embraced. It was at the foot of a hill steeply crowned with apples and a ruined fortress. Imagination did not make the world. Sweetness is the entire portion. Before anything could happen, happiness, the necessary precondition of the world, spoke and flowered over the hill. When I was in Hell on the ruined palisade, either mystery or loneliness kissed my open eyes. It felt hugely convex, seeing and immediately forgetting. By contrast, what I imagined later was nothing.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Before, What, Her

outputs.L1:
Before anything could happen—flecks of true gold upon her lips, her eyes more convex than any others'—the ground itself spoke, and the hedge of lilacs spoke in answer. What sang within the black tree was wholly gold. Her chair stood empty. This new absence was a vast shape, dark as the skin beneath a fruit's flesh. At the center of the earth, it enfolds and amplifies the dead, whose music never falters nor slows. She arrived by car; I arrived by train. We embraced at the foot of a hill crowned steeply with apple trees and a ruined fortress.

Imagination did not create the world. Sweetness is its whole inheritance. Before anything could happen, happiness—that necessary precondition of the world—spoke, and flowered across the hillside. When I stood in Hell, upon the ruined palisade, either mystery or loneliness pressed its kiss upon my open eyes. It felt immensely convex: to see, and in the same instant, to forget. Beside it, all I imagined afterward was nothing at all.
outputs.L2:
Prior to any event unfolding, genuine gold specks marked her lips, and her eyes bulged more than anyone else's—the earth itself gave voice, as did the lilac boundary. The blackened tree's song consisted purely of gold. Her seat sat vacant. This fresh void resembles some vast shape, dark like fruit's inner skin. Deep within the earth, this void encircles and magnifies the deceased, whose melody plays without pause.

By automobile she arrived; by rail, I did. Then we held each other close, there where a hill rose sharply, topped with apple trees and a crumbling stronghold. The world was never a creation of fantasy. Only sweetness constitutes the whole share. Before events could unfold, joy—that essential foundation upon which the world rests—found voice and bloomed across the slope.

During my time in Hell, upon that shattered rampart, something between enigma and solitude pressed lips against my unshielded eyes. The sensation was one of vast curvature, of witnessing and instantly losing the memory. Whatever I pictured afterward, in comparison, amounted to emptiness.
outputs.L3:
Before anything could happen, before the first gesture or word passed between them, the ground itself spoke, and beside it, a barrier of lilacs joined its voice to the earth's. Their speech was not sound but light—a golden imagery that traced itself along her mouth, settled in the hollows of her eyes, and climbed upward into the black tree where a song had taken root. The tree did not sing in the way birds sing; rather, it held the song within its darkness, as though music itself had found a body to inhabit, and that body was black wood reaching toward a sky indifferent to color.

Her chair, when the moment came to look for her, was empty. But this was no ordinary absence, no simple vacancy of wood and cushion. The emptiness took on shape, became a dark figure that did not merely occupy the space where she should have sat but expanded outward, surrounding everything, drawing into itself all the dead who lay at the center of the earth. It was as though her absence had become a kind of gravity, pulling the buried and the forgotten upward into its shadow, amplifying their silence until it filled the room where her chair sat empty and waiting.

Yet despite this absence, despite the dark figure and its terrible gathering of the dead, she did arrive—by car, while the narrator came by train, each carried toward the other by different engines, different roads. They met at last at the foot of a hill, a place crowned above with apple trees heavy with fruit and the broken stones of a ruined fortress, as though nature and human ambition had both reached upward toward the same height and both, in their own ways, had fallen into ruin and sweetness together. There, at the hill's foot, they embraced, and something in that embrace seemed to close the distance between the empty chair and this fullness of arrival.

It would be wrong, though, to say that imagination had conjured this world into being—the hill, the apples, the fortress, the meeting itself. Imagination did not create the world. Instead, happiness spoke first, happiness flowered over the hill like something growing wild and unbidden, and only because happiness had already spoken could the world exist at all. The flowering was not decoration upon an already-existing scene; it was the necessary precondition, the seed from which the hill, the fortress, and the lovers' embrace all grew. Without that prior blooming of joy, none of it—not the car, not the train, not the meeting at the hill's foot—could have come to pass.

But this joy was not without its shadow, its counterpart in ruin. In some other place, a place that felt hellish in its devastation, something happened to the narrator that resisted easy naming. Either mystery or loneliness—the two were nearly indistinguishable in that ruined landscape—reached out and kissed the narrator's open eyes. The kiss was intensely convex, curving outward in a way that seemed to press against the very shape of perception, an experience so full and so strange that it exceeded the ordinary flatness of seeing. And yet, almost as soon as it happened, it was forgotten—not faded slowly, but erased immediately, swallowed back into the ruin from which it had come. Afterward, whenever the narrator tried to imagine what that kiss might have been, to reconstruct it in memory or fantasy, those later imaginings felt like nothing at all, pale and hollow beside the vanished original, mere gestures toward an intensity that could not be recovered once it had slipped away into forgetting.
outputs.L4:
The fortress had lost its walls the way a mouth loses teeth—gradually, then all at once, until only the gums of stone remained, gray and gapped against the sky. She was standing where the gate had been, though there was no gate, only the memory of a threshold, an absence shaped like a door.

Gold flecks moved in the air between them. Not dust—something else, something that caught light and held it a half-second longer than dust should, like the light itself was reluctant to let go. He noticed her eyes first. Convex. Bulging slightly, as though pressed from the inside by everything she had ever looked at and never spoken.

"You came," she said, or he imagined she said it, and already the distinction was dissolving, the way a photograph dissolves if you stare too long into its grain.

Behind her, a black tree was singing. Not rustling—singing, a low continuous note that seemed to come from the bark itself, from some resonant chamber inside the trunk. He did not ask her about the tree. There are things you accept in ruins that you would never accept in rooms with proper ceilings.

"I don't remember how we met," she said.

"Neither do I."

This seemed to satisfy her, as if the not-remembering were itself a kind of bond, stronger than any origin story could have been. Origin stories, after all, are constructed afterward, stitched together from fragments the mind finds convenient. What had actually happened—the smell of the air, the temperature of a hand, the particular slant of afternoon—all of that was already gone, had been gone since the moment it occurred, replaced instantly by its own inadequate replica.

The gold flecks thickened between them, or seemed to. He reached toward one and it dissolved before his fingers closed, leaving nothing, not even the memory of texture.

"Try not to remember this," she said. "Just have it."

He didn't understand her, not with his mind, but something lower in him, something convex like her eyes, curved outward to receive the moment as it was: the black tree's note trembling in the ruined air, the gold light without source, her face neither beautiful nor plain but simply present, simply there, sweetness without narrative, sweetness without the scaffolding memory would later build around it and call understanding.

Already he could feel the forgetting beginning, soft as erosion. Already the fortress was reclaiming its silence, the tree quieting, the gold flecks dispersing into ordinary dust. Soon there would be only the story he told himself, thin and wrong, a photograph of a photograph.

But now—now the convexity of her gaze pressed against him like weather, like something not thought but felt, arriving whole and entire and already leaving, and this, only this, seemed to matter: not what he would carry away, which would be little and false, but what filled him in that instant, sweet and total and impossible to keep.
outputs.L5:
# Before

Before the words caught in her throat, there was silence—the kind that stretches between two people who have run out of easy things to say. She had rehearsed this moment a hundred times in the shower, in the car, in the quiet minutes before sleep. But rehearsal never prepares you for the weight of an actual room, an actual face waiting for you to speak.

## What

What could she possibly say that hadn't already been said, in different words, in different years? *What do you want from me?* had been asked so many times it had lost its meaning, become just sounds people made when they didn't know how to reach each other anymore. She wondered if there was a question underneath all the other questions—the real one, the one that mattered. What are we still doing here? What are we afraid of losing?

## Her

Her hands were steadier than she expected. That surprised her more than anything—that after everything, her body still knew how to be calm even when her mind was a storm. She looked at the person across from her, someone she had known for years and somehow still didn't fully understand, and she realized the question was never really about them at all.

It was about her. What she wanted. What she was willing to accept. What version of herself she'd be if she stayed, and what version she might become if she didn't.

Before she could change her mind, she spoke.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about arrival and reunion, using imagery of gold, lilacs, and a ruined fortress, with recurring phrases for effect.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Return

The gold came first—it always comes first—spilling through the fortress gaps like something remembered before it is seen. You arrive the way light arrives: already late, already forgiven.

I have been waiting in the shape of a doorway. I have been waiting in the shape of a doorway so long that the door forgot its hinges, the hinges forgot their iron, and still I stood there, a rectangle of patience cut from ruined stone.

The lilacs do not care about our history. They bloom anyway, purple mouths opening in the rubble, whispering their small sweet nothing into the collapsed throat of the west wall. This is April's argument against memory. This is April's argument against memory: that beauty does not need permission from the past to happen again.

You are walking toward me through the broken archway, and the gold is doing that thing gold does—turning every ordinary object into evidence of a miracle. Your coat. Your hands. The dust you disturb with each step, rising like small ghosts uncertain whether to celebrate or warn.

I have missed you in the specific way that stone missed its mortar, the specific way that towers missed their height. Not sentimentally. Structurally. As an absence that changes what can stand.

The fortress does not remember being whole. It only remembers becoming this—these fingers of wall reaching up into nothing, these arches that frame sky instead of ceiling. And yet the lilacs. And yet the lilacs, insisting.

You are close now. Close enough that I can see the gold is not sunlight but something you carry, something leaking from your sleeves like you've been swimming through a collapsed cathedral of it, some treasury dissolved to liquid, some crown melted down to travel easier.

I have been waiting in the shape of a doorway. Now the doorway becomes a question. Now the doorway becomes an opening, in every sense the word allows.

The lilacs release their purple into the space between us—closing it, the way scent closes distance, the way memory closes decades, the way your hand closing around mine closes some ancient argument the fortress has been having with the wind.

This is arrival: gold pooling at the threshold like something the ruins have been saving. This is reunion: two ghosts discovering they were never haunting different houses, only different rooms of the same broken magnificent one.

The walls do not need to stand to hold us. The walls do not need to stand to hold us; they only need to remember, once, holding something upright, some purpose, some king, some ceremony now indistinguishable from wind, from lilac, from the particular gold of your returning face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dreamlike piece of flash fiction that blends grief and encounter, incorporating repeated phrases like "before anything could happen."
counterfactuals.output:
The Waiting Room of Small Birds

Before anything could happen, my mother was already sitting at the kitchen table that no longer existed, peeling an orange that bled light instead of juice. The peel came away in one long spiral, the way she used to do it when I was young and believed unbroken things were lucky.

"You're not supposed to be here," I said, though I didn't know what here meant, only that the walls breathed like lungs and the window showed a field that hadn't grown anything since 1987.

Before anything could happen, she offered me a section of the orange. I almost took it. My hand moved on its own, the way hands do in the space between sleep and the story you tell yourself about sleep. But her fingers were made of the same light as the fruit, and I understood, the way you understand things only in dreams and funerals, that eating it would mean something permanent.

The birds began then—small brown ones, dozens, filling the corners of the room like punctuation. They didn't fly so much as flicker, here and then there, stitching the air with their bodies. My mother smiled at them like old friends.

"They're early," she said. "They're always early."

Before anything could happen, I asked her the question I'd rehearsed for three years—not the big question, not why or how, but the small one, the one about whether she'd been afraid. The birds went quiet. The orange stopped bleeding light. Even the field outside held its breath, waiting to see if grass would remember how to grow.

She looked at me the way she used to when I'd ask if monsters were real, that particular tenderness reserved for questions too large for their answers.

"Ask me something smaller," she said.

So I asked about the birds instead. She said they were the minutes we hadn't spent together, come home to roost. She said there were more of them than I would ever want to count, and that this was not a punishment but a kind of harvest.

Before anything could happen—before I could reach for her, before the orange could finish unraveling into whatever it was becoming, before the birds could either scatter or settle—the table folded itself back into the ordinary kitchen, gray morning light, the coffee maker gurgling its small mechanical grief.

I stood there a long moment, waiting to see if the room would remember what it had almost given me.

It didn't.

But on the counter, impossibly, sat a single curl of orange peel, unbroken, still faintly warm, as if something had, after all, begun to happen—and then, carefully, changed its mind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem exploring memory and mythic landscapes—gold trees, empty chairs, hills crowned with apples—in a tone reminiscent of Louise Glück.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Orchard at the End of Memory

I.

There was a hill once, crowned with apples,
and I was standing at the bottom of it
the way you stand at the bottom of anything
you have already lost—

looking up.

The trees were gold that year.
Not with autumn. With something else,
some permanent condition
the light had agreed to.

I did not climb.
Some doors you honor by not opening.

II.

In the house below the hill
there was a chair no one sat in.
This is not a metaphor.
Or it is only the metaphor
that everything becomes,
given enough time alone in a room.

The chair faced the window.
Someone had arranged it that way
on purpose, long ago,
so that whoever wasn't coming
would have a view.

III.

Memory is not the hill.
Memory is the persistence of the hill
after the season that made it
has already left the earth—

the way a name stays in a mouth
after the person it belonged to
has stopped answering to anything.

I call this fidelity.
Others might call it refusal.

IV.

The apples never fell.
This is the part I return to,
the impossible part:
gold, and gravity suspended,
as if the tree understood
that to let go was to admit
an ending, and the tree
was not yet ready
to become a story.

I was not ready either.

V.

Somewhere a chair keeps facing a window.
Somewhere a hill keeps its gold
through every version of winter.
This is what the mind does
with what it cannot carry down the hill:

it leaves the whole thing standing,
lit, useless, magnificent—

a museum with one visitor
who comes back every night
to stand in the doorway
and not go in.

VI.

I am telling you this
because the dead require accuracy,
not devotion.
The trees were gold. The chair was empty.
The hill did not care
whether I climbed it.

That is the myth I have made
from an afternoon:
that the past is a country
with perfect weather
and no road back—

only this looking,
which is its own kind of arrival,
which is the only harvest
I was ever offered.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, abstract narrative about two people meeting after loss, using rich sensory metaphors and a nonlinear structure.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Water Remembers

I.

The room holds its breath the way a shell holds the sea—
not the ocean itself, but the shape memory makes
when something vast has left.

You arrive smelling of rain that hasn't fallen yet,
and I recognize you before I understand
that recognition is just an old wound
learning a new alphabet.

II.

*(Before this, or after—time is a liar with a soft voice)*

There was a kitchen once. Yellow light.
Someone's hands around a mug that steamed
like a small ghost trying to escape upward.
We do not speak of this. We speak of it constantly,
in the way we hold our coffee now, four years
or four minutes later, the cup between us
like a held breath, like a held thing.

III.

Grief is a language with no future tense.
Only the eternal present of *was*—
the photograph that keeps developing
in the dark room of the sternum,
image sharpening long after the flash has died.

But look: your hand on the table.
Look: the specific weight of afternoon
gathering in the corners like something
that wants to be called dust, or light,
or evidence that time is still passing
through us, patient as a river
through a canyon it is slowly,
gently, without malice, destroying.

IV.

I keep circling back to the door.
Not this one—the other one.
The one that closed on a version of me
that still doesn't know
what it's lost.

That version is still in the yellow kitchen.
That version is still holding
onto Tuesday like a raft.

V.

Here is what nobody says about the after:
it is not empty. It is full
the way a held note is full—
vibrating with the absence
of the next sound, but ringing,
ringing, ringing.

You sit across from me now
(is it now? has it always been now?)
and I see in you the same architecture—
rooms built around a missing center,
the way a wound organizes the whole body
around its own healing.

VI.

We do not talk about the dead.
We talk about the weather in the year we lost them,
how the leaves turned early that autumn,
too early, as if the trees themselves
were trying to warn us.

We talk about salt—
how the body makes its own ocean
when it has nowhere else to put the water.

VII.

*(This happens first. This happens last. Choose your own devastation.)*

Your fingers wrap the mug.
Steam rises like something ascending,
like a soul, if you believe in that sort of architecture.

I think: this is what remains
after the flood recedes—
not the absence of water
but the changed shape of the land,
the new rivers cut into what
used to be simple ground.

VIII.

We are two people who have learned
the terrible fluency of loss,
speaking now in the dialect of survivors—
half silence, half the specific gravity
of a look that says *I know, I know, I know*
without needing the exhausting scaffolding
of further words.

IX.

Outside, the rain that hadn't fallen yet
finally falls.

It sounds like applause
for something we didn't know
we'd survived.

X.

The room still holds its breath.
But now there are two shells here,
two shapes where the ocean used to be,
sitting close enough
that if you listened—
if you really listened—

you might hear us
becoming, slowly,
weather.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short surrealist text meditating on absence and sweetness, where nature and death intertwine, ending with a reflection on imagination versus reality.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Bees Remember

The honey remembers a flower that no longer exists. It pools in the comb like amber light, sweetness distilled from something already gone—the way grief tastes, sometimes, of clover.

In the orchard where my grandmother is buried, the trees have grown strange fruit: small, translucent, shaped like closed eyes. When they fall, they do not bruise. They simply dissolve into the grass, leaving behind a residue that smells of rain and old paper. The crows will not touch them. Even scavengers know the difference between nourishment and memory.

I have seen a deer stop mid-stride in a clearing, one hoof lifted, and simply cease—not fall, not die in any way I recognize, but fold inward like a map returning to its pocket. Where it stood, mushrooms bloomed in a perfect ring by morning, pale and patient, feeding on whatever the deer had decided to leave behind.

This is how the world unmakes and remakes its sweetness: through absence, through the terrible generosity of things that stop being.

I keep a jar of the honey on my windowsill. Some nights I convince myself I can see the flower inside it—white, five-petaled, trembling—though I know this is only light bending through glass, only my mind performing its small necessary magic.

But perhaps that is the only difference that matters: not between the living and the dead, but between what we invent to survive the missing, and the plain, indifferent fact of the jar, the shelf, the window, the dark beyond it—asking nothing of us, offering nothing back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
